Research report | Evidence through 22 October 2026 Chinese edition

AI is changing work; job replacement depends on more than capability

For internet-company workers, the useful question is not whether a job title is safe, but which parts of the job can be delegated and what happens to the remaining work. The evidence shows task change and entry-level hiring pressure, not a reliable replacement rate for all workers.[1][2]

This report's practical conclusion: assess whole workflows before drawing staffing conclusions. Faster production matters only if the result is accepted, useful and economical after review. For individuals, build evidence that you can solve a business problem with AI, including recognizing when its answer is wrong.

1 / What the evidence measures

Exposure is a reason to investigate, not a count of lost jobs

ILO/NASK's May 2025 global task-based assessment places 25% of employment in occupations potentially exposed to generative AI. This measures possible task change, not observed displacement.[1]

A job combines outputs, decisions and obligations. A tool that drafts one output does not necessarily handle the exceptions, obtain approval or take responsibility for the result. The following distinctions prevent a capability estimate from quietly becoming a claim about unemployment.

Four measures answer four different questions
MeasureQuestion answeredWhat it cannot establish alone
ExposureCould AI affect the tasks in this occupation?Whether employers have adopted it or removed positions.
UseWhich activities appear in actual AI interactions?Whether the work was accepted or needed fewer people.
ProductivityHow much useful work is completed for the resources spent?Whether demand will expand enough to retain or add staff.
EmploymentWhat happens to hiring, jobs, exits or unemployment?How much of the change AI caused rather than other forces.

Microsoft Research's July 2025 study of 200,000 Bing Copilot conversations found information gathering and writing prominent among activities users sought help with. Its occupational applicability measure is not an employment-loss estimate.[5]

Use this distinction when interpreting a headline: first identify what was counted, then ask whether the study actually followed workers or only classified tasks. A percentage without that distinction is a poor basis for a career or staffing decision.

2 / Changes already observed

A weaker entry route can matter before mass layoffs appear

Payroll observation

A gap against peer growth, not a share of all jobs destroyed

Stanford's August 2026 revision uses US ADP payrolls through June: employment among 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations was 19% below a path matching less-exposed peers' growth, mainly through lower hiring. This is descriptive, not causal or economy-wide job loss; education and pre-existing trends complicate attribution.[2]

Labor-market analysis

Unemployment answers a different question

Anthropic's March 2026 analysis combined Claude-based exposure with US labor-survey data. It found no systematic unemployment increase among highly exposed workers since late 2022, but tentative evidence of slower younger-worker hiring. This earlier, different outcome does not contradict the later payroll gap.[3]

One employer's account

At one growing AI company, hiring shifted and staff supervised more AI work

Anthropic's October 2026 internal study reports junior technical hires' share falling from 27% to 9% since early 2025, alongside more AI supervision work. These are shares, not absolute job losses. Internal records and 17 interviews at a fast-growing AI vendor do not represent the sector.[4]

The practical interpretation is narrower than either alarm or reassurance. A company can keep incumbent staff while making fewer offers to newcomers. A falling junior share can also reflect faster senior recruitment. To distinguish these possibilities in your organization, inspect absolute junior hires, total hires, departures and transfers together, against comparable periods and business demand.

For new entrants, the question is therefore not just whether vacancies exist, but what experience those vacancies require. For managers, removing routine work also raises a training question: if beginners no longer perform it, where will they learn to recognize mistakes? This is a work-design risk to investigate, not evidence that junior employees have become unnecessary.

3 / Productivity without a universal multiplier

Measure accepted work, not how fast a draft appears

Experiments depend on the tools, tasks and period tested

METR's February 2026 update recalls an early-2025 randomized experiment in which experienced open-source developers took longer with AI. Its later experiment covered 57 developers and over 800 tasks; participant/task selection and time measurement made current gains hard to estimate. Neither result is a universal coding coefficient.[6]

Self-reports estimate perceived value, not a measured speedup

METR surveyed 349 technical workers in February-April 2026, asking them to estimate how much value their work created with AI compared with without it. The medians across three questions ranged from 1.4 to 2 times. This is perceived value, not speed on the same tasks; the nonrandom survey does not establish a measured workforce productivity gain.[7]

These findings warrant measurement, not a single verdict that AI helps or hurts everyone. The relevant unit for a team is a completed piece of work that meets the same requirements. A shorter first draft is valuable if review and correction do not consume the saving; extra output is valuable if someone actually needs it.

Separate two questions in a pilot. Can we finish comparable work with less total effort? And can we now do worthwhile work that we previously could not justify? The first concerns efficiency; the second concerns a change in the work selected. Mixing them makes it hard to tell whether a tool saved time, expanded scope or simply produced more material.

4 / Why task automation is not a staffing formula

The missing link is what the business does with saved effort

The following is this report's explanatory synthesis, not a measured causal model. Even when a task can be delegated, staffing depends on the cost of completing the whole workflow and on whether there is valuable additional demand.

This explains why neither "AI can write the code" nor "people must still approve it" settles the employment question. Approval may remain essential while requiring fewer people than implementation did. Conversely, cheaper implementation may make a previously unaffordable product viable. The decision turns on actual demand and remaining work, not on whether any human task survives.

Accountability is also not a permanent technical advantage. An organization can keep a human responsible while automating much of the preparation. Workers therefore need to understand both the decisions they own and how much labor those decisions will require, rather than treating responsibility as a guarantee of unchanged headcount.

5 / Internet-company roles

Compare tasks within six role families, not risk scores between titles

The mapping below is this report's conditional analysis, not six measured occupational forecasts. It identifies candidate tasks, work that still needs an accountable owner, and evidence that would justify a change. The conditions must be tested with the tools, data and quality requirements of the actual team.

Consider a weekly business report. AI can prepare a SQL draft, but the result is useful only after someone checks which users it counts, whether the data is current and what the comparison means. If accepted reports arrive faster without more correction, routine extraction could require fewer hours; staffing still depends on additional demand and the work that remains. This is an illustrative workflow, not an observed employment effect.

Engineering

Candidate delegation: Well-specified code changes, test drafts and documentation, where reliable tests and repository context are available.

Role shift to test: Less time writing each change; more attention to requirements, architecture, security and failure diagnosis. Staffing pressure is more plausible if accepted delivery accelerates without a corresponding expansion in valuable projects.

Watch: Time to accepted release, reviewer effort, escaped defects and rollback work. Lines of code alone cannot answer the staffing question.

Data analysis

Candidate delegation: SQL drafts, recurring report assembly and initial chart commentary, if metric definitions and permitted data access are explicit.

Role shift to test: More work defining the business question, checking data and separating correlation from cause. Routine reporting roles face more pressure if stakeholders can obtain trusted answers without an analyst handling every request.

Watch: Reconciliation errors, decision turnaround and whether recommendations survive source checking, not just the number of dashboards produced.

Product management

Candidate delegation: Draft specifications, feedback grouping and prototype preparation, provided customer evidence and constraints are available.

Role shift to test: Less document production; greater emphasis on choosing problems, resolving tradeoffs and coordinating commitments. Fewer handoffs may become possible, but generating a plausible requirement does not establish that customers need it.

Watch: Time from evidence to decision, requirement reversals and outcomes after release, rather than specification volume.

Design and content

Candidate delegation: Copy variants, resizing and routine layout exploration when brand rules, rights and acceptance criteria are clear.

Role shift to test: More selection, editing and user research. Standardized production may need fewer hours; new demand for tailored material may absorb some savings. Neither implies that all creative work is protected or replaceable.

Watch: Accepted assets per total work hour, revision cycles, accessibility and audience response. Generating more alternatives is not itself a better result.

Operations and marketing

Candidate delegation: Campaign variants, routine monitoring and report preparation where data is reliable and actions have clear limits.

Role shift to test: More experiment design, budget judgment and exception handling. If execution becomes cheaper, the scarce work may be deciding which activity is worth funding, rather than launching more of it.

Watch: Incremental business results, spend, policy violations and correction effort. Do not attribute every change in conversions to AI use.

Customer support

Candidate delegation: Classification and standard answers when the knowledge base is current and escalation works.

Role shift to test: Human work concentrates on exceptions, disputes and service recovery. Stable ticket demand plus reliable automated resolution could reduce staffing needs; unresolved cases merely moved out of view would not be a genuine saving.

Watch: Repeat contacts, reopened cases, resolution quality and total cost per resolved issue, including escalations.

Across these roles, a useful career strategy is to connect execution with an outcome you can evaluate. That does not mean abandoning technical or craft expertise: without enough subject knowledge, it is difficult to tell whether a convincing output is actually correct. It means making the value of that expertise visible in decisions and accepted results.

6 / 2030 and the longer term

Prepare for different paths; no single forecast settles your role

WEF's 2025 employer-survey projection spans over 1,000 companies, 22 industries and 55 economies: 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced globally by 2030 across multiple macrotrends. These are projected jobs, not realized changes or AI-only effects.[8]

Anthropic Institute's September 2026 US scenario model links 2030 outcomes to capability, adoption and adjustment assumptions. It supplies conditional outcomes, not forecast probabilities; version 1.0 omits policy responses and business cycles, among other forces.[9]

For an internet company, the following are planning scenarios developed for this report, not predictions borrowed from those totals. Their value is in identifying what would change a decision.

If assistance improves but review remains demanding

Job titles may persist while daily tasks change substantially. Teams should invest in clear inputs and acceptance criteria, then test whether review effort falls as well as drafting time. If it does not, increasing output targets could simply transfer pressure to reviewers.

If reliable delegation spreads across workflows

Smaller teams could cover a broader scope, and some handoff-heavy roles could be combined. Whether that reduces employment depends on whether new products and customers absorb the capacity. Watch completed delivery per team alongside the project backlog and customer demand, not tool adoption alone.

If substitution outpaces new demand and retraining

Pressure could extend beyond routine work to experienced staff, with fewer entry routes and harder transitions between roles. A response would need actual destination work, paid learning time and transition support, not merely a requirement to learn a tool. Current evidence cannot assign a credible probability or date to this path.

Beyond 2030, the uncertainty is larger, not a reason for a more precise number. Continued capability gains would still leave questions about deployment cost, trust, customer demand and institutional choices. This evidence set cannot support a single long-term replacement rate, a permanently safe profession, or a claim that today's exposure ranking will remain fixed.

7 / Decisions you can make now

Audit a workflow, run a bounded comparison, then decide

The following are recommendations to test locally, not reported gains. An individual can start with their own work; a team lead can add shared quality standards and staffing data. Neither should upload confidential material to an unapproved service to perform the exercise.

  1. List work as deliverables, not job labels. For a normal working period, record recurring outputs, frequency, time spent, recipients and acceptance criteria. Identify where errors become expensive and which tasks depend on information that is unavailable to the tool. This reveals where delegation is feasible without pretending to calculate a personal replacement probability.
  2. Choose one repeatable workflow with a clear fallback. Define success before trying AI. Compare similar work with and without assistance where practical; random assignment is preferable when feasible, otherwise record differences in complexity and experience. Include failed attempts and exceptions rather than selecting only impressive examples. Keep permission to publish, spend or change production systems separate from permission to draft.
  3. Count all effort until acceptance. Track preparation, prompting, review, corrections and handoffs, plus tool charges. Record elapsed delivery time separately from active labor time. Compare work accepted to the same standard per total labor hour, and check the relevant business outcome. A small pilot may establish feasibility without proving a general productivity effect.
  4. Protect the route from beginner to independent contributor. For individuals, retain examples showing how you detected an error, checked evidence and improved an outcome. For managers, assign supervised end-to-end work and assess reasoning, not merely polished output. Track junior offers and progression in absolute numbers as well as shares; a stable total headcount can conceal a narrowing entry route.
  5. Make the next decision conditional on the result. If quality deteriorates or review consumes the saving, narrow the task or stop. If quality holds and total cost falls, decide explicitly whether to use capacity for more demand, service improvement, retraining or a staffing change. A positive tool trial alone is not a sufficient case for a headcount reduction.

The most useful evidence for your next career or team decision is a traceable result: what work was accepted, what it cost to produce, and what became possible because of it.

8 / How far these findings travel

Use this as a research synthesis, not a forecast for Chinese tech employment

This report synthesizes nine accessible primary-source pages available in the research snapshot, with an evidence cutoff of 22 October 2026. The snapshot records retrieval at 13:46 UTC that day. It combines task estimates, usage studies, payroll observations, experiments, a self-report survey, an employer case and forward-looking work; their numbers are not pooled because they measure different populations and outcomes.

Much of the evidence concerns US workers, global occupations or specific products and employers. It does not directly estimate employment effects in Chinese internet companies. Differences in tool access, language performance, labor costs, regulation, customer demand and management practices could change both adoption and staffing responses. Transfer the questions and measurement approach; test the magnitudes locally.

The collection is selected evidence, not an exhaustive literature review. Vendor research is useful but not independent corroboration of its own product claims. Only accessible content is used: the WEF citation is its public release, and inaccessible pages or linked papers are not treated as read. Findings, this report's interpretations and future scenarios are separated throughout.
